cf.title: pgcrypto crypt() can return text with invalid encoding

input.subject: BUG #19600: pgcrypto crypt() can return text with invalid encoding

verdict_reasoning: The goal and the design copy what pgp_*_decrypt_text already do, and no objection survived at levels 1a or 1b. The one surviving objection, standards-compat-1, is a fixable back-branch question: crypt(pw, stored_hash) starts to raise an error for stored hashes that hold invalid encoding. A committer who knows pgcrypto has to decide between master only and back branches.

brief.title: pgcrypto: reject crypt() results that are invalid in the database encoding
brief.problem: crypt() copies a fixed number of salt bytes into its text result, so a multibyte character that straddles the cut leaves a truncated sequence in the output. The server stores that text, but upper() then fails on it and COPY cannot reload it. Any user can trigger this, because crypt() is executable by PUBLIC; the documented gen_salt() idiom cannot, since gen_salt() emits ASCII only.
brief.proposed_design: pg_crypt() calls pg_verifymbstr() on the result before it returns it, as pgp_sym_decrypt_text and pgp_pub_decrypt_text already do. A truncated result now raises "invalid byte sequence for encoding". The patch adds a crypt-utf8 regression test that non-UTF8 databases skip.
user_visible_surface: crypt() raises "invalid byte sequence for encoding" when its result would hold a truncated multibyte sequence.
crypt(pw, stored_hash) raises an error for stored hashes that already hold invalid encoding, for the right password and for a wrong one.
author_claims: The reporter says this is the same class of bug the earlier pgp_*_decrypt_text fix covered, but crypt() has no bytea variant to fall back on.
The reporter says traditional DES copies 2 salt bytes, xDES copies 9 and MD5 copies up to 8, so the cut point differs by algorithm.
The reviewer reports that ASCII salts and valid multibyte salts return the same hashes as before the patch.
The reviewer reports that SHA-crypt and Blowfish already reject non-ASCII salts.
The reviewer reports the patch applies cleanly to REL_18 and REL_19, and to REL_14 through REL_17 with Makefile adjustments, but did not build them.
brief.thread_state: The reporter, the author and one reviewer took part, and the reviewer tested the patch and called it good. The reviewer asked for xDES and MD5 test cases and a release-note mention of stored hashes that will now fail; the author has not replied.
unclear: The material does not say whether the fix goes to back branches, given that existing stored hashes start to raise errors after a minor upgrade.
The material does not say how users with affected stored hashes should find or repair them.
The material does not say whether gen_salt() or the pgcrypto documentation changes; no documentation hunk is attached.
The material does not say whether rejecting non-ASCII salts up front, as SHA-crypt and Blowfish do, was considered.

prior_attempts.title: Encoding protection for pgcrypto
prior_attempts.reason: The visible messages do not show why. Cary Huang reported failing tests and questioned aborting the transaction instead of issuing a warning. The author posted v2 and argued that callers who want no encoding check can use the bytea variants, and no later message follows.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P2 added pg_verifymbstr() to pgp_sym_decrypt_text and pgp_pub_decrypt_text; this proposal adds the same check to crypt(), which has no bytea variant. Message #3 reports that this check later went in as d536aee5566.

objections.title: Back-patching turns working password checks into errors after minor upgrade
objections.failure_scenario: A site stored DES or MD5 hashes made with a hand-written non-ASCII salt. After a minor upgrade, `where pwhash = crypt($1, pwhash)` raises an error instead of returning false, so those users cannot log in. Any query that evaluates crypt() over several rows fails as a whole if one row holds such a hash.
objections.argument: Message #3 says these hashes stop working for the right password and for a wrong one, and that crypt() has no bytea variant to fall back on. Message #3 also checked that the patch applies to REL_14 through REL_19, but the thread has not decided whether to back-patch. Committers usually keep minor releases free of changes that make working queries fail. The proposal also gives no way to find or rehash affected rows before upgrading, and the author has not replied to the release-note request.
objections.author_must_show: Will this go to master only, and if back-patched, what query lets users find affected stored hashes before the upgrade, and how do they rehash them?

critic.reasoning: Message #3 confirms that stored invalid hashes raise an error for right and wrong passwords, and it calls the trade-off acceptable. The thread does not decide on back-patching or give a way to find affected rows, so the objection stands as fixable.

refuted.title: Back-patch turns already stored hashes into errors at minor upgrade
refuted.failure_scenario: An application stores crypt(pw, salt) hashes built from a non-ASCII salt, and those rows survive through pg_upgrade or physical replicas. After a minor release with this fix, every login check calls crypt(pw, stored_hash), which now raises an error for these users. The operator finds out when those logins start failing in production.
refuted.argument: Message #3 confirms that stored invalid hashes raise an error for both right and wrong passwords, and that the patch applies to REL_14 through REL_19. COPY cannot reload such rows, but pg_upgrade and physical standbys copy relation files unchanged, so the data can exist today. The reviewer judged the trade-off acceptable and asked for a release-note mention, but the author has not answered. The proposal does not say whether it goes to back branches or how users can find affected rows before they upgrade.
refuted.author_must_show: Will this go only to master, or, if back-patched, what query lets users find and rehash affected stored hashes before the minor upgrade?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. Its point that pg_upgrade and physical standbys keep such rows alive supports that objection but is not a separate one.

refuted.title: Back-patching turns unrestorable hashes into failed logins after a minor update
refuted.failure_scenario: An application stored crypt() hashes built from a hand-written non-ASCII salt and checks passwords with crypt(pw, stored_hash). After a minor update that carries this fix, every check for those users raises an error, even with the right password. Users cannot log in, and the release notes give no query to find or repair the affected rows.
refuted.argument: Message #3 shows the patch applies to REL_14 through REL_19 but was not built there, and it confirms that existing invalid hashes stop working. Before the fix, these rows fail only on logical dump and restore or on text functions. Many sites use physical backups and never hit that failure. Back branches usually avoid behaviour changes that break working applications, and the thread does not discuss a master-only fix or a detection query.
refuted.author_must_show: Will this go to master only, or to back branches with a release-note query that finds stored hashes holding invalid encoding?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. It describes the same failed logins after a minor update and asks the same question about master-only versus back branches.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: No format change, but stored hashes with invalid encoding survive pg_upgrade and then make crypt() raise an error.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: Back-patching turns working password checks into errors after minor upgrade

touch_points.label: pg_dump / restore round-trip
touch_points.reason: The fix stops crypt() from producing text that COPY cannot reload; rows already stored stay unrestorable.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: crypt() is executable by PUBLIC, so any user can store invalid text today; the patch closes that path.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: Message #3 checked REL_14 through REL_19; a back-patch makes existing password checks raise an error after a minor upgrade.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: Small: one pg_verifymbstr() call in pg_crypt() and one regression test with an alternative expected file for non-UTF8 databases.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Should this fix go to master only, or also to REL_14 through REL_19, where existing stored hashes start to raise errors after a minor upgrade?
What query lets users find stored crypt() hashes that hold invalid encoding before they upgrade?
How should a user rehash an affected row, given that crypt(pw, stored_hash) now raises an error even for the right password?
Was rejecting non-ASCII salts up front for DES, xDES and MD5 considered, as SHA-crypt and Blowfish already do?
Will the next version add the xDES and MD5 test cases and the release-note text that message #3 asked for?

committability.owner_note: No committer has spoken in the thread. It needs someone who knows pgcrypto and the back-branch policy for behaviour changes.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the back-branch decision: failed logins on sites with affected stored hashes after a minor upgrade, and the release-note text. The code itself is one check that copies existing pgcrypto practice.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted the patch on the day of the report but has not answered the review in message #3, about two weeks old at the review date.

priority.reason: Only callers who pass a hand-written non-ASCII salt to DES, xDES or MD5 crypt() are affected, and the 4.3 KB patch touches pgcrypto only. One reviewer tested it and called it good; what remains is a committer's decision on back branches.

provisional_note: The code was not read. The claim that the check reads only the finished result, and so leaves valid hashes unchanged, rests on message #3; the back branches were checked for applicability but not built.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Upgrade pgcrypto to crypt_blowfish 1.3
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch ports upstream crypt_blowfish 1.3 into pgcrypto so that crypt() recognizes bcrypt hashes with the $2b$ prefix (and $2y$), keeping the Postgres-specific local changes. An earlier version only mapped $2b$ to the $2a$ code path, which Daniel Gustafsson rejected because the two variants handle the old bug differently.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No reviewer took up the patch after it was added to the commitfest. After a cursory review and a fix for gcc warnings, it was returned in a batch of entries that lacked reviewer interest, with no objection to the patch itself.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Rather than code changes, what this patch needs is more
community interest.

precedents_retrieved.title: Encoding protection for pgcrypto
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes pgp_sym_decrypt_text and pgp_pub_decrypt_text check that the decrypted result is valid in the database encoding, and raise an error if it is not. It adds regression tests for this and moves some existing tests that failed under some encodings.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Cary Huang reported failing tests and questioned aborting the transaction instead of issuing a warning. The author posted v2 and argued that callers who want no encoding check can use the bytea variants, and no later message follows.

precedents_retrieved.title: Rename "getdatabaseencoding()" to "pg_database_encoding()", and document
precedents_retrieved.summary: Rename the undocumented SQL function getdatabaseencoding() to pg_database_encoding(), to match pg_client_encoding(), and document it. psql tab completion would switch to current_setting('server_encoding').
precedents_retrieved.objection: Daniel Gustafsson noted that extensions call the function, and Tom Lane said the old name would not be removed without a multi-year deprecation period. Tom Lane also judged a cosmetic rename not worth the effort. The author dropped the rename and offered a documentation-only patch, which Thom Brown questioned because he would rather deprecate the function.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There are plenty of ugly and inconsistent names in Postgres,
and an enormous amount of more-valuable work to do.

precedents_retrieved.title: Clarify the comments about varlena header encoding
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch rewrites the comments in postgres.h that describe the bit layouts of varlena headers, so readers do not misread the length word, the alignment notes or the size of a TOAST pointer. Version 2 adds a 0b prefix to the bit patterns and mentions the type tag next to the TOAST pointer layout.
precedents_retrieved.objection: John Naylor found that both versions made the comments harder to read. In his view, adding the type tag pulls the comment away from its purpose, which is to show how the first byte tells what kind of varlena follows. He judged the current text a local maximum that small edits would likely make worse, and doubted that any change was needed. The author did not reply for four weeks, so Michael Paquier marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
More broadly, I think the description of varlenas in this header is at
a kind of "local maximum" -- minor adjustments are more likely to make
it worse.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert COPY OUT to follow the pre-8.3 handling of ASCII control characters, namely that \r, \n, \t, \b, \f, \v are dumped as those two-character...
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert COPY OUT to follow the pre-8.3 handling of ASCII control characters, namely that \r, \n, \t, \b, \f, \v are dumped as those two-character representations rather than a backslash and the literal control character. I had made it do the other to save some code, but this was ill-advised, because dump files in which these characters appear literally are prone to newline mangling.  Fortunately, doing it the old way should only cost a few more lines of code, and not slow down the copy loop materially. Per bug #3795 from Lou Duchez.

This reverts the non-text (custom/directory/tar) output format support
for pg_dumpall added by 763aaa06f03 and its feature-specific follow-ups,
in line with Noah Misch's post-commit review which recommends reverting
and finishing the work through the commitfest.

Scope is deliberately minimal: only the feature itself is removed.
Independent improvements that merely touched the same files, or that were
committed alongside the feature but do not depend on its design, are
preserved.

Reverted (the feature):

  763aaa06f03  Add non-text output formats to pg_dumpall
  d6d9b96b404  Clean up nodes that are no longer of use in 007_pgdumpall.pl
  01c729e0c7a  Fix casting away const-ness in pg_restore.c
  c7572cd48d3  Improve writing map.dat preamble
  3c19983cc08  pg_restore: add --no-globals option to skip globals
  abff4492d02  Fix options listing of pg_restore --no-globals
  bb53b8d359d  Fix small memory leak in get_dbname_oid_list_from_mfile()
  a793677e57b  pg_restore: Remove dead code in restore_all_databases()
  a198c26dede  pg_dumpall: simplify coding of dropDBs()
  ec80215c033  pg_restore: Remove unnecessary strlen() calls in options parsing

Preserved (independent of the feature):

  b2898baaf7e  the check_mut_excl_opts() helper in src/fe_utils/option_utils.c
               and its use in pg_dump
  7c8280eeb58  pg_dump's conflicting-option refactor (and tests 002/005)
  be0d0b457cb  pg_dumpall's rejection of --clean together with --data-only
               (re-expressed directly, since pg_dumpall.c is otherwise
               returned to its pre-feature state)
  74b4438a70b  the dangling-grantor-OID GRANT fix (back-patched through 16)
  273d26b75e7, d4cb9c37765  independent pg_restore.sgml clarifications

Because the feature restructured pg_dumpall.c and pg_restore.c (pg_restore's
main() was split into restore_one_database() plus a dispatcher) and
interleaved its option checks with the conflicting-option refactor in the
same regions, the cosmetic check_mut_excl_opts() reflow of those two files'
option blocks is inseparable from the feature and comes out with it; the
behavior is unchanged.  The reusable helper and pg_dump's use of it are
unaffected.

precedents_retrieved.title: NOT VALID for Unique Indexes
precedents_retrieved.summary: Simon Riggs proposed allowing an existing index to be switched between unique and non-unique via ALTER INDEX SET [NOT] UNIQUE [NOT VALID] and ALTER INDEX VALIDATE UNIQUE, so uniqueness could be added without a long write-excluding scan and validated later in a separate transaction. The WIP patch added a new pg_index column (induniquevalid) and did not yet implement the index validation scan.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No deciding objection was raised; reviewers were positive and asked only design questions. The author said he could not finish the patch for the next commitfest and would complete it later, and a later message noted the patch no longer applied to HEAD and asked for an updated version, with no reply shown. The entry was left incomplete with no updated version posted.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I won't be able to finish this patch in time for this next CF, but
thanks for your interest, I will complete for PG15 later this year.

roaster_notes.note: The only precedent, [P2], is the same check on other pgcrypto functions, and its reason is recorded only as an AI summary. That summary names two concerns: tests failing under some encodings, and raising an error where a warning might do. This patch adds a skip file and was tested in UTF8, LATIN1 and SQL_ASCII databases. Message #3 weighed the error-versus-warning trade-off for crypt(), which has no bytea fallback, and judged it acceptable. Whether the fix should go to back branches, given that stored hashes start to fail after a minor upgrade, falls under the backpatchability angle, not prior attempts.

The contract change itself fits existing practice: pgp_*_decrypt_text already validates its text result. No new syntax, GUC or catalog object is added. The fix also restores the pg_dump and COPY round-trip.
Apart from existing stored data, the patch changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol or extension ABI. Standbys and subscribers are not affected differently from the primary.

From the security angle there is nothing to object to. The patch removes the one case where an unprivileged user can store text that is invalid in the database encoding through crypt(), and it adds no new privilege, exposure or default. The new error shows only bytes the caller would have received anyway, and the lockout of already-stored invalid hashes is an upgrade and back-branch question for other angles.

Beyond the back-branch question, the maintenance and fit cost is small. The check copies an existing pgcrypto practice, adds negligible work to a function that is slow by design, and adds no API or new mechanism.

No existing feature does this job. The gen_salt() idiom avoids the bug only when callers use it, and crypt() has no bytea variant, so nothing stops invalid text reaching a table. The patch reuses pg_verifymbstr(), the check pgp_*_decrypt_text already use, so it extends an existing mechanism and does not add a second one.

This is a bug fix. crypt() stores text that is invalid in the database encoding, and then upper() and COPY reload fail on it, so demand needs no proof from field reports. The cost falls only on callers who pass non-ASCII salts. The real question is the effect on already stored hashes in back branches, which belongs to the compatibility angle.
